entries.70ef29f279914bc0d3adb54d482291de37176c4b: <div sID="gen7845" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="20" osisID="1Chr.20" sID="1Chr.20"/> <div eID="gen7845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7846" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7847" type="x-p"/> Here is a repetition of the story of David's wars, I. With the Ammonites, and the taking of Rabbah, <reference osisRef="1Chr.20.1-1Chr.20.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. With the giants of the Philistines, <reference osisRef="1Chr.20.4-1Chr.20.8">ver. 4-8</reference>.
entries.38d313979bdd6a763df8e7788d2cfbc10d3df65d: <div eID="gen7847" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen7846" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Defeat of the Ammonites. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1306.)</title> <div sID="gen7848" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And it came to pass, that after the year was expired, at the time that kings go out <hi type="italic">to battle,</hi> Joab led forth the power of the army, and wasted the country of the children of Ammon, and came and besieged Rabbah. But David tarried at Jerusalem. And Joab smote Rabbah, and destroyed it. <hi type="super">2</hi> And David took the crown of their king from off his head, and found it to weigh a talent of gold, and <hi type="italic">there were</hi> precious stones in it; and it was set upon David's head: and he brought also exceeding much spoil out of the city. <hi type="super">3</hi> And he brought out the people that <hi type="italic">were</hi> in it, and cut <hi type="italic">them</hi> with saws, and with harrows of iron, and with axes. Even so dealt David with all the cities of the children of Ammon. And David and all the people returned to Jerusalem. <div eID="gen7848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7849" type="x-p"/> How the army of the Ammonites and their allies was routed in the field we read in the foregoing chapters. Here we have the destruction of Rabbah, the metropolis of their kingdom (<reference osisRef="1Chr.20.1">v. 1</reference>), the putting of their king's crown upon David's head (<reference osisRef="1Chr.20.2">v. 2</reference>), and the great severity that was used towards the people, <reference osisRef="1Chr.20.3">v. 3</reference>. Of this we had a more full account in <reference osisRef="2Sam.11.1-2Sam.12.31">2 Sam. xi., xii.</reference>, and cannot but remember it by this sad token, that while Joab was besieging Rabbah David fell into that great sin in the matter of Uriah. But it is observable that, though the rest of the story is repeated, that is not: a hint only is given of it, in those words which lie here in a parenthesis—<hi type="italic">But David tarried at Jerusalem.</hi> If he had been abroad with his army, he would have been out of the way of that temptation; but, indulging his ease, he fell into uncleanness. Now, as the relating of the sin David fell into is an instance of the impartiality and fidelity of the sacred writers, so the avoiding of the repetition of it here, when there was a fair occasion given to speak of it again, is designed to teach us that, though there may be a just occasion to speak of the faults and miscarriages of others, yet we should not take delight in the repetition of them. That should always be looked upon as an unpleasing subject which, though sometimes one cannot help falling upon, yet one would not choose to dwell upon, any more than we should love to rake in a dunghill. The persons, or actions, we can say no good of, we had best say nothing of.
entries.522405325a86a5d4b54e1cb735bf21fe06b08608: <div eID="gen7849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7850" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> And it came to pass after this, that there arose war at Gezer with the Philistines; at which time Sibbechai the Hushathite slew Sippai, <hi type="italic">that was</hi> of the children of the giant: and they were subdued. <hi type="super">5</hi> And there was war again with the Philistines; and Elhanan the son of Jair slew Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite, whose spear staff <hi type="italic">was</hi> like a weaver's beam. <hi type="super">6</hi> And yet again there was war at Gath, where was a man of <hi type="italic">great</hi> stature, whose fingers and toes <hi type="italic">were</hi> four and twenty, six <hi type="italic">on each hand,</hi> and six <hi type="italic">on each foot:</hi> and he also was the son of the giant. <hi type="super">7</hi> But when he defied Israel, Jonathan the son of Shimea David's brother slew him. <hi type="super">8</hi> These were born unto the giant in Gath; and they fell by the hand of David, and by the hand of his servants. <div eID="gen7850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7851" type="x-p"/> The Philistines were nearly subdued (<reference osisRef="1Chr.18.1">ch. xviii. 1</reference>); but, as in the destruction of the Canaanites by Joshua the sons of Anak were last subdued (<reference osisRef="Josh.11.21">Josh. xi. 21</reference>), so here in the conquest of the Philistines the giants of Gath were last brought down. In the conflicts between grace and corruption there are some sins which, like these giants, keep their ground a great while and are not mastered without much difficulty and a long struggle: but judgment will be brought forth unto victory at last. Observe, 1. We never read of giants among the Israelites as we do of the giants among the Philistines-giants of Gath, but not giants of Jerusalem. The growth of God's plants is in usefulness, not in bulk. Those who covet to have <hi type="italic">cubits added to their stature</hi> do not consider that it will but make then more unwieldy. In the balance of the sanctuary David far outweighs Goliath. 2. The servants of David, though men of ordinary stature, were too hard for the giants of Gath in every encounter, because they had God on their side, who takes pleasure in abasing lofty looks, and mortifying the giants that are in the earth, as he did of old by the deluge, though they were men of renown. Never let the church's friends be disheartened by the power and pride of the church's enemies. We need not fear great men against us while we have the great God for us. What will a finger more on each hand do, or a toe more on each foot, in contest with Omnipotence? 3. These giants <hi type="italic">defied Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Chr.20.7">v. 7</reference>) and were thus made to pay for their insolence. None are more visibly marked for ruin that those who reproach God and his Israel. God will do great things rather than suffer the enemy to <hi type="italic">behave themselves proudly,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.32.27">Deut. xxxii. 27</reference>. The victories of the Son of David, like those of David himself, are gradual. <hi type="italic">We see not yet all things put under him;</hi> but it will be seen shortly: and death itself, the last enemy, like these giants, will be triumphed over.  <chapter eID="1Chr.20"/> <div eID="gen7851" type="x-p"/>

entries.b7cc2bd7df91ea1f9a4c06990f66a19704acf832: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3819"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 20</title> <div sID="gen5482" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Chr.20.1-1Chr.20.3">1Ch 20:1-3</reference>. Rabbah Besieged by Joab, Spoiled by David, and the People Tortured.<div eID="gen5482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5483" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3819"/><hi type="bold">1. at the time when kings go out to battle--</hi>in spring, the usual season in ancient times for entering on a campaign; that is, a year subsequent to the Syrian war.<div eID="gen5483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5484" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Joab led forth the power of the army, and wasted the country ... of Ammon--</hi>The former campaign had been disastrous, owing chiefly to the hired auxiliaries of the Ammonites; and as it was necessary, as well as just, that they should be severely chastised for their wanton outrage on the Hebrew ambassadors, Joab ravaged their country and invested their capital, Rabbah. After a protracted siege, Joab took one part of it, the lower town or "city of waters," insulated by the winding course of the Jabbok. Knowing that the fort called "the royal city" would soon fall, he invited the king to come in person, and have the honor of storming it. The knowledge of this fact (mentioned in <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.26">2Sa 12:26</reference>) enables us to reconcile the two statements--"David tarried at Jerusalem" (<reference osisRef="1Chr.20.1">1Ch 20:1</reference>), and "David and all the people returned to Jerusalem" (<reference osisRef="1Chr.20.3">1Ch 20:3</reference>). <div eID="gen5484" type="x-p"/>
entries.1f86306eac92be0feb865d775ea42209dc63229b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3820"/><div sID="gen5485" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3820"/><hi type="bold">2. David took the crown of their king ..., and found it to weigh a talent of gold--</hi>equal to one hundred twenty-five pounds. Some think that Malcom, rendered in our version "their king," should be taken as a proper name, Milcom or Molech, the Ammonite idol, which, of course, might bear a heavy weight. But, like many other state crowns of Eastern kings, the crown got at Rabbah was not worn on the head, but suspended by chains of gold above the throne.<div eID="gen5485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5486" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">precious stones--</hi>Hebrew, a "stone," or cluster of precious stones, which was set on David's head. <div eID="gen5486" type="x-p"/>
entries.d9e8c78f4d790a59b1e938423e4ad37a0d0a0857: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3821"/><div sID="gen5487" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3821"/><hi type="bold">3. cut them with saws, &c.--</hi>The Hebrew word, "cut them," is, with the difference of the final letter, the same as that rendered "put them," in the parallel passage of Samuel [2Sa 12:31]; and many consider that putting them to saws, axes, and so forth, means nothing more than that David condemned the inhabitants of Rabbah to hard and penal servitude.<div eID="gen5487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5488" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Chr.20.4-1Chr.20.8">1Ch 20:4-8</reference>. Three Overthrows of the Philistines and Three Giants Slain. <div eID="gen5488" type="x-p"/>
entries.0bb29d0e637ca9e41bf96265efcf3c2babd48d98: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3822"/><div sID="gen5489" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3822"/><hi type="bold">4. war at Gezer--</hi>or Gob (see <reference osisRef="2Sam.21.18-2Sam.21.22">2Sa 21:18-22</reference>). <chapter eID="1Chr.20"/>

entries.99eecbe837da8f3cbf36cbf2f1ed5b1cea50d417: <div eID="gen13701" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen13702" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13703" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13703" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13702" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13704" type="x-p"/> Joab smites the city of Rabbah; and David puts the crown of its king upon his own head, and treats the people of the city with great rigour, <reference osisRef="1Chr.20.1-1Chr.20.3">1Chr 20:1-3</reference>. First battle with the Philistines, <reference osisRef="1Chr.20.4">1Chr 20:4</reference>. Second battle with the Philistines, <reference osisRef="1Chr.20.5">1Chr 20:5</reference>. Third battle with the Philistines, <reference osisRef="1Chr.20.6">1Chr 20:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.20.7">1Chr 20:7</reference>. In these battles three giants are slain, <reference osisRef="1Chr.20.8">1Chr 20:8</reference>. <div eID="gen13704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13705" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen13705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13706" type="x-p"/> After the year was expired, at the time that kings go out to battle - About the spring of the year; see the note on <reference osisRef="2Sam.11.1">2Sam 11:1</reference>. <div eID="gen13706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13707" type="x-p"/> After this verse the parallel place in Samuel relates the whole story of David and Bath-sheba, and the murder of Uriah, which the compiler of these books passes over as he designedly does almost every thing prejudicial to the character of David. All he states is, but David tarried at Jerusalem; and, while he thus tarried, and Joab conducted the war against the Ammonites, the awful transactions above referred to took place.
entries.85492c42bb2766f67442a9af25034c339abf7791: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen13707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13708" type="x-p"/> David took the crown of their king - off his head - See <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.30">2Sam 12:30</reference>. <div eID="gen13708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13709" type="x-p"/> Precious stones in it - The Targum says, "And there was set in it a precious stone, worth a talent of gold; this was that magnetic stone that supported the woven gold in the air." What does he mean?
entries.09a080698307f1995de6774c3d53230e91bda284: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen13709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13710" type="x-p"/> He brought out the people - See this transaction particularly explained in the notes on the parallel places, <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.30-2Sam.12.31">2Sam 12:30-31</reference> (note).
entries.378f6e5a0213bc44431c30643d7d5e2d0252d993: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen13710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13711" type="x-p"/> Elhanan the son of Jair - See the note on <reference osisRef="2Sam.21.19">2Sam 21:19</reference>. The Targum says, "David, the son of Jesse, a pious man, who rose at midnight to sing praises to God, slew Lachmi, the brother of Goliath, the same day on which he slew Goliath the Gittite, whose spear-staff was like a weaver's beam."
entries.62fc7d90d806ebaceb244286abdea5b6da2bff08: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen13711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13712" type="x-p"/> Fingers and toes were four and twenty - See the note on <reference osisRef="2Sam.21.20">2Sam 21:20</reference>.
entries.40f28478ccc858b68abc16cad1b60f70950b85c3: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen13712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13713" type="x-p"/> These were born unto the giant in Gath - "These were born להרפא leharapha, to that Rapha in Gath, or to Arapha." So the Vulgate, Septuagint, and Chaldee. <div eID="gen13713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13714" type="x-p"/> The compiler of these books passes by also the incest of Amnon with his sister Tamar, and the rebellion of Absalom, and the awful consequences of all these. These should have preceded the fourth verse. These facts could not be unknown to him, for they were notorious to all; but he saw that they were already amply detailed in books which were accredited among the people, and the relations were such as no friend to piety and humanity could delight to repeat. On these grounds the reader will give him credit for the omission. See on <reference osisRef="1Chr.20.1">1Chr 20:1</reference> (note).  <chapter eID="1Chr.20"/> <div eID="gen13714" type="x-p"/>

entries.c3cb7a7b5a3d1a45a8620f05e5b0f36edb623c23: <reference osisRef="1Chr.20.1-1Chr.20.8">1Ch 20:1-8</reference> <div eID="gen5805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5806" type="x-p"/> The account of the siege of Rabbah, the capital, in the following year, <reference osisRef="1Chr.20.1-1Chr.20.3">1Ch 20:1-3</reference>, is much abridged as compared with that in <reference osisRef="2Sam.11.1">2Sa 11:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.26">2Sa 12:26</reference>-31. After the clause, “but David sat (remained) in Jerusalem,” in 2 Sam 11, from <reference osisRef="2Sam.11.2">2Sa 11:2</reference> onwards, we have the story of David’s adultery with Bathsheba, and the events connected with it (2 Sam 11:3-12:25), which the author of the Chronicle has omitted, in accordance with the plan of his book. Thereafter, in <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.26">2Sa 12:26</reference>, the further progress of the siege of Rabbah is again taken up with the words, “And Joab warred against Rabbah of the sons of Ammon;” and in <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.27-2Sam.12.29">2Sa 12:27-29</reference> the capture of that city is circumstantially narrated, viz., how Joab, after he had taken the water-city, i.e., the city lying on both banks of the upper Jabbok (the Wady Ammân), with the exception of the Acropolis built on a hill on the north side of the city, sent messages to David, and called upon him to gather together the remainder of the people, i.e., all those capable of bearing arms who had remained in the land; and how David, having done this, took the citadel. Instead of this, we have in the Chronicle only the short statement, “And Joab smote Rabbah, and destroyed it” (<reference osisRef="1Chr.20.1">1Ch 20:1</reference>, at the end). After this, both narratives (<reference osisRef="1Chr.20.2">1Ch 20:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.20.3">1Ch 20:3</reference>, and <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.30">2Sa 12:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.31">2Sa 12:31</reference>) coincide in narrating how David set the heavy golden crown of the king of the Ammonites on his head, brought much booty out of the city, caused the prisoners of war taken in Rabbah and the other fenced cities of the Ammonites to be slain in the cruellest way, and then returned with all the people, i.e., with the whole of his army, to Jerusalem. Thus we see that, according to the record in the Chronicle also, David was present at the capture of the Acropolis of Rabbah, then put on the crown of the Ammonite king, and commanded the slaughter of the prisoners; but no mention is made of his having gone to take part in the war. By the omission of this circumstance the narrative of the Chronicle becomes defective; but no reason can be given for this abridgment of the record, for the contents of <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.26-2Sam.12.31">2Sa 12:26-31</reference> must have been contained in the original documents made use of by the chronicler. On the differences between <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.31">2Sa 12:31</reference> (Sam.) and <reference osisRef="1Chr.20.3">1Ch 20:3</reference> of the Chronicle, see on 2Sa 12:31. ויּשׂר, “he sawed asunder,” is the correct reading, and ויּשׂם in Samuel is an orthographical error; while, on the contrary, בּמּגרות in the Chronicle is a mistake for בּמגזרות in Samuel. The omission of בּמּלבּן אותם והעביר is probably explained by the desire to abridge; for if the author of the Chronicle does not scruple to tell of the sawing asunder of the prisoners with saws, and the cutting of them to pieces under threshing instruments and scythes, it would never occur to him to endeavour to soften David’s harsh treatment of them by passing over in silence the burning of them in brick-kilns. <div eID="gen5806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5807" type="x-p"/> The passages parallel to the short appendix-like accounts of the valiant deeds of the Israelitish leaders in <reference osisRef="1Chr.20.4-1Chr.20.8">1Ch 20:4-8</reference> are to be found, as has already been remarked, in <reference osisRef="2Sam.21.18">2Sa 21:18</reference>-22. There, however, besides the three exploits of which we are informed by the chronicler in <reference osisRef="2Sam.21.15-2Sam.21.17">2Sa 21:15-17</reference>, a fourth is recorded, and that in the first place too, viz., the narrative of David’s fight with the giant Jishbi-Benob, who was slain by Abishai the son of Zeruiah. The reason why our historian has not recounted this along with the others is clear from the position which he assigns to these short narratives in his book. In the second book of Samuel they are recounted in the last section of the history of David’s reign, as palpable proofs of the divine grace of which David had had experience during his whole life, and for which he there praises the Lord in a psalm of thanksgiving (2 Sam 22). In this connection, David’s deliverance by the heroic act of Abishai from the danger into which he had fallen by the fierce attack which the Philistine giant Jishbi-Benob made upon him when he was faint, is very suitably narrated, as being a visible proof of the divine grace which watched over the pious king. For the concluding remark in <reference osisRef="2Sam.21.17">2Sa 21:17</reference>, that in consequence of this event his captains adjured David not to go any more into battle along with them, that the light of Israel might not be extinguished, shows in how great danger he was of being slain by this giant. For this reason the author of the book of Samuel has placed this event at the head of the exploits of the Israelite captains which he was about to relate, although it happened somewhat later in time than the three exploits which succeed. The author of the Chronicle, on the contrary, has made the account of these exploits an appendix to the account of the victorious wars by which David obtained dominion over all the neighbouring peoples, and made his name to be feared among the heathen, as a further example of the greatness of the power given to the prince chosen by the Lord to be over His people. For this purpose the story of the slaughter of the Philistine giant, who had all but slain the weary David, was less suitable, and is therefore passed over by the chronicler, although it was contained in his authority,<note placement="foot">Lightfoot says, in his <hi type="italic">Chronol. V. T.</hi> p. 68: <hi type="italic">Illud praelium, in quo David in periculum venit et unde decore et illaesus exire non potuit, omissum est</hi>.</note> as is clear from the almost verbal coincidence of the stories which follow with 2Sa 21:18. The very first is introduced by the formula, “It happened after this,” which in 2nd Samuel naturally connects the preceding narrative with this; while the chronicler has retained אהרי־כן as a general formula of transition, - omitting, however, עוד (Sam.) in the following clause, and writing ותּעמוד, “there arose,” instead of ותּהי. עמד in the later Hebrew is the same as קוּם. The hypothesis that ותעמד has arisen out of עוד ותּהי (in Samuel) is not at all probable, although עמד is not elsewhere used of the origin of a war. Even קוּם is only once (<reference osisRef="Gen.41.30">Gen 41:30</reference>) used of the coming, or coming in, of a time. On בּגזר and ספּי instead of בּנב and סף, see on 2Sa 21:18. ויּכּנעוּ at the end of the fourth verse is worthy of remark, “And they (the Philistines) were humbled,” which is omitted from Samuel, and “yet can scarcely have been arbitrarily added by our historian” (Berth.). This remark, however, correct as it is, does not explain the omission of the word from 2nd Samuel. The reason for that can scarcely be other than that it did not seem necessary for the purpose which the author of the book of Samuel had in the first place in view. As to the two other exploits (<reference osisRef="1Chr.20.6-1Chr.20.8">1Ch 20:6-8</reference>), see the commentary on <reference osisRef="2Sam.21.19">2Sa 21:19</reference>-22. אל for אלּה in the closing remark (<reference osisRef="1Chr.20.8">1Ch 20:8</reference>) is archaic, but the omission of the article (אל instead of האל, as we find it in <reference osisRef="Gen.19.8">Gen 19:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.19.25">Gen 19:25</reference>, and in other passages in the Pentateuch) cannot be elsewhere paralleled. In the last clause, “And they fell by the hand of David, and by the hand of his servants,” that David should be named is surprising, because none of those here mentioned as begotten of Rapha, i.e., descendants of the ancient Raphaite race, had fallen by the hand of David, but all by the hand of his servants. Bertheau therefore thinks that this clause has been copied <hi type="italic">verbatim</hi> into our passage, and also into <reference osisRef="2Sam.21.22">2Sa 21:22</reference>, from the original document, where this enumeration formed the conclusion of a long section, in which the acts of David and of his heroes, in their battles with the giants in the land of the Philistines, were described. But since the author of the second book of Samuel expressly says, “These four were born to Rapha, and they fell” (<reference osisRef="2Sam.21.22">2Sa 21:22</reference>), he can have referred in the words, “And they fell by the hand of David,” only to the four above mentioned, whether he took the verse in question unaltered from his authority, or himself added אלּה את־ערבּעת. In the latter case he cannot have added the בּיד־דּוד without some purpose; in the former, the reference of the בּיד־דּוד in the “longer section,” from which the excerpt is taken, to others than the four giants mentioned, to Goliath perhaps in addition, whom David slew, is rendered impossible by אלּה את־ערבּעת. The statement, “they fell by the hand of David,” does not presuppose that David had slain all of them, or even one of them, with his own <hi type="italic">hand</hi>; for בּיד frequently signifies only through, i.e., by means of, and denotes here that those giants fell in wars which David had waged with the Philistines - that David had been the main cause of their fall, had brought about their death by his servants through the wars he waged. The Numbering of the People, the Pestilence, and the Determination of the Site for the Temple - 1 Chronicles 21-22:1 <div eID="gen5807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5808" type="x-p"/> The motive which influenced the king, in causing a census of the men capable of bearing arms throughout the kingdom to be taken in the last year of his reign, has already been discussed in the remarks on 2 Sam, where we have also pointed out what it was which was so sinful and displeasing to God in the undertaking. We have, too, in the same place commented upon the various stages of its progress, taking not of the differences which exist between the numbers given in <reference osisRef="2Sam.24.9">2Sa 24:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.24.13">2Sa 24:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.24.24">2Sa 24:24</reference>, and those in our record, <reference osisRef="1Chr.21.5">1Ch 21:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.21.12">1Ch 21:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.21.25">1Ch 21:25</reference>; so that here we need only compare the two accounts somewhat more minutely. They correspond not merely in the main points of their narrative of the event, but in many places make use of the same terms, which shows that they have both been derived from the same source; but, as the same time, very considerable divergences are found in the conception and representation of the matter. In the very first verse, David’s purpose is said in 2nd Samuel to be the effect of the divine anger; in the Chronicle it is the result of the influence of Satan on David. Then, in <reference osisRef="2Sam.24.4-2Sam.24.9">2Sa 24:4-9</reference>, the numbering of the people is narrated at length, while in the Chronicle, <reference osisRef="1Chr.21.4-1Chr.21.6">1Ch 21:4-6</reference>, only the results are recorded, with the remark that Joab did not complete the numbering, Levi and Benjamin not being included, because the king’s command was an abomination to him. On the other hand, the Chronicle, in <reference osisRef="1Chr.21.19-1Chr.21.27">1Ch 21:19-27</reference>, narrates the purchase of Araunah’s threshing-floor for a place of sacrifice, and gives not merely a more circumstantial account of David’s offering than we find in Samuel (<reference osisRef="2Sam.24.19-2Sam.24.25">2Sa 24:19-25</reference>), but also states, in conclusion (vv. 28-30), the circumstances which induced David to offer sacrifice even afterwards, on the altar which he had built at the divine command, on the threshing-floor bought of Araunah. The purpose which the author of the Chronicle had in view in making this concluding remark is manifest from <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.1">1Ch 22:1</reference>, which should properly be connected with 1 Chron 21: “And David said, Here is the house of Jahve God, and here the altar for the burnt-offering of Israel.” Only in this verse, as Bertheau has correctly remarked, do we find the proper conclusion of the account of the numbering of the people, the pestilence, and the appearance of the angel, and yet it is omitted in the book of Samuel; “although it is manifest from the while connection, and the way in which the history of David and Solomon is presented in the books of Samuel and Kings, that the account is given there also only to point out the holiness of the place where Solomon built the temple even in the time of David, and to answer the question why that particular place was chosen for the site of the sanctuary.” This remark is perfectly just, if it be not understood to mean that the author of our book of Samuel has given a hint of this purpose in his narrative; for the conclusion of <reference osisRef="2Sam.24.25">2Sa 24:25</reference>, “And Jahve was entreated for the land, and the plague was stayed,” is irreconcilable with any such idea. This concluding sentence, and the omission of any reference to the temple, or to the appointment of the altar built on the threshing-floor of Araunah to be a place of sacrifice for Israel, and of the introductory words of the narrative, “And again the wrath of Jahve was kindled against Israel, and moved David against them,” (<reference osisRef="2Sam.24.1">2Sa 24:1</reference>), plainly show that the author of the book of Samuel regarded, and has here narrated, the event as a chastisement of the people of Israel for their rebellion against the divinely chosen king, in the revolts of Absalom and Sheba (cf. the remarks on <reference osisRef="2Sam.24.1">2Sa 24:1</reference>). The author of the Chronicle, again, has without doubt informed us of the numbering of the people, and the pestilence, with its results, with the design of showing how God Himself had chosen and consecrated this spot to be the future place of worship for Israel, by the appearance of the angel, the command given to David through the prophet Gad to build an altar where the angel had appeared, and to sacrifice thereon, and by the gracious acceptance of this offering, fire having come down from heaven to devour it. For this purpose he did not require to give any lengthened account of the numbering of the people, since it was of importance to him only as being the occasion of David’s humiliation.  <chapter eID="1Chr.20"/> <div eID="gen5808" type="x-p"/>
